title: How to Use a Massage Gun: Heads, Speed and Time per Muscle — cv.cm
description: How to use a massage gun safely: which attachment to pick, start on low speed, 10–30 s per spot and 1–2 min per muscle, and where never to use it.
h1: How do you use a massage gun safely?
answer: Turn the massage gun on at its lowest speed before it touches you, rest it on a large muscle without pushing, and glide it slowly along the muscle. Spend 10–30 seconds on any one spot and no more than 1–2 minutes per muscle. Keep it off bones, joints, the head, the front and sides of the neck, the spine and behind the knee.

body: A massage gun, also called a percussion or percussive massager, is a handheld device with a head that moves quickly in and out, usually 30 to 50 times per second. It taps the muscle in short, fast pulses. Many people find it eases the feeling of tight or tired muscles, and some use it as part of a warm-up or cool-down.

It is a self-care tool for large, healthy muscles in adults. It does not diagnose or treat injuries, and more force is not better. Most problems with massage guns come from pressing too hard, staying too long, or using them on the wrong part of the body.
Read the manual for your own device first. Speeds, attachments and warnings differ by model, and the maker's warnings come before any general guide, including this one.

body: If you are not sure, use the ball. It works for almost every area in this guide and is the most forgiving if you press a little too hard.

sections.h: How to use it step by step

ol: Pick a large muscle you can reach comfortably, such as the front of the thigh. Sit or stand so the muscle is relaxed, not tensed.
Choose the lowest speed. Turn the device on before you place it on the body.
Rest the head on the muscle at about 90° to the skin. Do not push down: let the weight of the device do the work. Pressing harder can bruise the muscle.
Glide slowly along the length of the muscle, about 2–3 cm per second, in long passes.
If you find a tight spot, pause there for 10–30 seconds, then keep moving. Do not hold on one spot for minutes.
Stop after 1–2 minutes on that muscle. Move to the next muscle or turn the device off before lifting it away.
Raise the speed only on a later session, and only if the low speed felt comfortable the next day.

body: Pressure in words: light means the head rests on the skin and the muscle barely moves; medium means you can see the muscle ripple; firm means you lean in slightly. For most people, light to medium is enough. Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning, tingling or electric pain means stop at once.
A whole-body session rarely needs more than 10 minutes. A timer such as cv.cm's countdown helps you keep to 1–2 minutes per muscle.

body: Before exercise, 30–60 seconds per muscle you are about to use is enough, followed by your usual warm-up. After exercise, use light pressure for 1–2 minutes per muscle. After very hard leg exercise, it is wise to wait or go very lightly, because one study found soreness slightly higher in the treated leg for a few hours.

sections.h: Where never to use a massage gun

ul: The head and face, and the front and sides of the neck (the throat and the large blood vessels there). Makers' manuals warn against use on the head, face, throat and neck.
The spine and directly on any bone: the collarbone, shoulder blade edges, kneecap, shin bone, hip bones, tailbone, ribs and elbow and ankle bones. On bone the device bounces and can hurt or bruise.
Joints: the front and back of the knee, elbow crease, wrist, armpit and groin.
Behind the knee, where large nerves and blood vessels run close to the surface.
Over bruises, cuts, rashes, burns, swelling, a recent injury or a surgical scar or implant hardware.
Over varicose veins, a swollen or painful calf, or any area that feels numb or has reduced feeling.
The abdomen, the genital area, and the eyes.

body.note: A swollen, warm, red or painful calf can be a sign of a blood clot (deep vein thrombosis). Never use a massage gun on it. Get medical help the same day, and call emergency services if you also have chest pain or shortness of breath.

sections.h: Who should ask a doctor first
body: Device makers list conditions where you should get medical advice before use, or not use the device at all. Check your own manual. Common ones include:

ul: a pacemaker, implanted defibrillator or other implanted electronic device, or metal implants in the area
a history of blood clots, deep vein thrombosis or embolism, or taking blood thinners
a bleeding disorder, or bruising easily
osteoporosis or osteopenia, or a recent or possible fracture
uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart, liver or kidney disease
diabetes or any nerve condition with numbness or reduced feeling
pregnancy (ask your midwife or doctor before any use)
cancer, tumors, or any recent surgery or injury

body: In rare cases, too much percussion on large muscles has caused serious muscle damage. A 2021 case report described a young woman with an untreated health condition who developed rhabdomyolysis, a dangerous breakdown of muscle, after about ten minutes of massage gun use on both thighs following cycling. Dark brown or tea-colored urine, severe muscle pain or swelling, or weakness after use needs emergency care.

Research on massage guns is new and small. A 2020 study of 16 healthy young men found that 5 minutes on the calf raised ankle range of motion by about 18% right after use, without lowering calf strength. A 2024 study of 65 active adults found that 5 minutes on the calf after hard exercise made little difference to strength, range of motion, endurance or soreness compared with resting.

A fair summary: a massage gun may give a short-term increase in flexibility and many people find it pleasant, but there is little evidence that it speeds recovery, prevents injury or treats pain conditions. It is not a substitute for seeing a doctor or physical therapist about an injury.

ul: Pressing down hard: you feel bruised or sore the next day. Fix: rest the device on the muscle, halve the speed and halve the time.
Holding on one spot for minutes: the spot becomes tender. Fix: keep it moving and pause no more than 30 seconds.
Starting on high speed: the muscle tenses against it. Fix: always start on the lowest setting.
Chasing pain near the spine or neck: risk of hitting bone or nerves. Fix: stay on the fleshy part of the muscle, at least two finger-widths from the spine.
Using it on a fresh injury: it can make swelling and bruising worse. Fix: wait, and get the injury checked if it does not improve.

faq.q: How long should you use a massage gun per session?
faq.a: Spend 1–2 minutes on each muscle and keep the whole session to about 10 minutes. Longer sessions add risk without clear benefit.

faq.q: Can I use a massage gun every day?
faq.a: Many people use one daily at light pressure for short times. If a muscle is still sore or bruised from the last session, skip it until it feels normal.

faq.q: Is it safe to use a massage gun on my neck?
faq.a: Do not use it on the front or sides of the neck or on the spine. Some people use the lowest speed briefly on the top of the shoulder muscle, well below the skull and away from the neck bones.

faq.q: Should I use a massage gun before or after a workout?
faq.a: Either can work. Before exercise, use 30–60 seconds on each muscle you will use, then warm up as usual. After very hard exercise, keep it light and short.

faq.q: Why do I feel sore after using a massage gun?
faq.a: You probably pressed too hard, used a high speed, or stayed too long on one area. Mild soreness should fade in a day or two; severe pain, swelling or dark urine needs a doctor at once.
